context.question_prompt: What does the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus say?

answer:
The course outline lists the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus as a core topic of Module 5, split into Part I (differentiating an accumulation function) and Part II (evaluating definite integrals using antiderivatives), but the materials I can see here don't include the actual formal statement of either part, so I can't quote it to you.

Not from your course materials: Part I says that if f is continuous, then F(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is differentiable and F′(x) = f(x). Part II says that for any antiderivative G of f, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = G(b) − G(a).

Before we go further: in your own words, what does Part I tell you about the relationship between the area function and the original function f?

passages.passage_text:
By the end of the course, a successful student will be able to:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{SLO\arabic*.}, leftmargin=2.6em]
\item \textbf{Model discrete and continuous change.} Translate a verbal description of a
      biological or social process into a recurrence equation, a limit statement, a
      derivative, or a definite integral, and interpret the mathematical result back in
      the original context.
\item \textbf{Evaluate limits and determine continuity} of algebraic, exponential,
      logarithmic, and trigonometric functions, including limits at infinity and limits
      that require the sandwich theorem.
\item \textbf{Differentiate} elementary, polynomial, rational, power, exponential,
      logarithmic, and trigonometric functions using the formal definition and the rules
      of differentiation (sum, product, quotient, chain, implicit).
\item \textbf{Apply derivatives} to find extrema, analyze monotonicity and concavity,
      solve optimization and related-rates problems, evaluate indeterminate forms
      (L'H\^{o}pital's Rule), and produce derivative-informed graphs.
\item \textbf{Evaluate definite and indefinite integrals}, state and apply both parts of
      the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, and interpret a definite integral as
      cumulative change or an average value.
\item \textbf{Use technology} (graphing calculators or spreadsheets) to visualize
      functions and data, iterate recurrence equations, and implement simple numerical
      methods (bisection, Newton--Raphson).
\item \textbf{Communicate quantitative reasoning}, including the assumptions behind a
      mathematical model, its limitations, and how well it fits real or simulated data.
\end{enumerate}

\MajorTopics
\begin{itemize}
\item The definite integral: the area problem, the general theory of Riemann integrals, properties (including optional order properties)
\item The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Parts I and II (with an optional rigorous treatment via Leibniz's Rule); antiderivatives and indefinite integrals
\item Applications: cumulative change, average values, and (optional) the Mean-Value Theorem for integrals, areas, volumes of solids, and rectification of curves
\end{itemize}
\KeyConcepts
Riemann sums; the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums / signed
area / accumulated change; linearity and additivity of the integral; the
Fundamental Theorem of Calculus (both parts); the indefinite integral;
average value of a function; area between curves; volumes of revolution;
arc length.
\LearnObj
\begin{enumerate}
\item Construct and evaluate Riemann sums and interpret the definite integral as their limit.
\item Apply properties of the definite integral (linearity, additivity, comparison).
\item Apply the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to evaluate definite integrals and to differentiate accumulation functions.
\item Compute indefinite integrals of standard functions.
\item Use integration to compute cumulative change and average values (e.g.\ total drug dose, average population size).
\item * Compute areas between curves, volumes of solids of revolution, and arc length.
\end{enumerate}
\PreReq Antiderivatives (Sec.\ 5.10); limits (Chapter 3, for the Riemann-sum limiting process).
\Hard The rigorous construction of the Riemann integral (Sec.\ 6.1.2) and
the proof of the Fundamental Theorem via Leibniz's Rule (Sec.\ 6.2.2*) are
the most abstract material so far; volume and arc-length integrals (Sec.\
6.3.5*--6.3.6*) require strong three-dimensional/geometric visualization
that many students have not practiced since high-school geometry.
